venues.n: ITC Grand Chola, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A Chola-temple palace in stone — the world's largest LEED Platinum hotel, and the definitive luxury address in the south.
Chennai's grande dame since 1974 — classic Taj service in the heart of the city, and home to the legendary Southern Spice.
A Chettinad-inspired palace on the Bay of Bengal — Chennai's only true seafront luxury hotel, opulent and calm.
An intimate design-led Hyatt conceived as a 'house of weavers' — and home to The Flying Elephant, the city's landmark bar.

venues.n: Taj Fisherman's Cove Resort & Spa, Chennai
venues.d: A beach resort inside a Dutch fort's ancient walls — 48 garden acres and a private beach on the Bay of Bengal.
A polished, genuinely green city hotel — among India's pioneering ECOTEL-certified luxury addresses, central and well-run.
A long-standing, well-placed IHG hotel in leafy Alwarpet — home to a much-loved South Indian dining room in Dakshin.
A bright, capable Hyatt Regency on Anna Salai — big rooms, a rooftop bar and dependable international service.
Modern South Indian reimagined as a chandelier-lit tasting menu — India's most awarded southern kitchen, and a genuine reason to cross the country.
A loving revival of Kerala home cooking — tapioca, jackfruit and bird's-eye chilli, from 800 recipes gathered across the state.
The definitive fine South Indian dining room — the four southern states on one silver-service menu, in the city that knows them best.
Regal South Indian dining since the 1980s — the four southern states on one grand menu, with appalams poured tableside.
ITC's celebrated North-West Frontier grill — dal Bukhara simmered overnight, kebabs and breads from the clay tandoor, eaten by hand.
The South Indian vegetarian institution that went global — the birthplace of the mini-idli, and a benchmark for the everyday classics.
The idli specialist beloved across the city — feather-soft idlis with a spread of chutneys and a peppery kaara kuzhambu, on a banana leaf.
Since 1948 — the modest Triplicane café whose sambar drowns its idlis and whose name generations of Chennai grew up on.
A serene, service-led vegetarian institution run by volunteers — refined Indian cooking with proceeds to charity, run 'with love'.

The soul of old Madras — a 7th-century Shiva temple whose 120-foot eastern gopuram rises in a riot of painted stucco gods over the lanes of Mylapore, its inner shrines still thick with camphor and jasmine. Go early for the aarti, then walk the four car-streets around the great temple tank. If you come in Panguni (mid-March to mid-April) the Arupathimoovar festival carries the 63 Nayanmar saints in grand procession through the neighbourhood.

The oldest quarter of Chennai, walked properly: the temple tank at dawn, the flower market where sellers thread mounds of jasmine and marigold, the Sunday morning Kapaleeshwarar precinct, and the narrow agraharam streets that end at the sea and San Thome. A private heritage guide turns an hour's stroll into the whole story of how a Tamil fishing town became a city — best in the cool of early morning.

A soaring white neo-Gothic cathedral built over the tomb of the Apostle St Thomas, who is believed to have been martyred in Mylapore in the 1st century — one of only three churches in the world raised over the resting place of an apostle. The gleaming spire is a landmark of the Santhome seafront; the crypt and small museum below make it a quiet, moving stop for every faith.

The world's second-longest urban beach — 13 kilometres of sand and a six-kilometre promenade where all of Chennai comes to walk at sunrise and eat sundal and bajji at dusk. Grand as the crowds are, it is the great democratic stage of the city; a private early-morning walk before the heat, past the fishing catamarans being hauled in, is the way to feel it.

The only lighthouse in India you can ride to the top of — a 46-metre tower on the Marina fitted with an electric elevator, opening onto a ninth-floor gallery with 360-degree views over the Bay of Bengal and the whole sweep of the beach and city skyline. A small, unexpected pleasure, best at golden hour when the coast lights up.

The finest collection of Chola bronzes on earth — some 1,500 lost-wax icons from the 9th to 13th centuries, crowned by the Nataraja of Tiruvalangadu and the Ardhanarisvara of Tiruvenkadu, the cosmic dancer and the god-goddess in a single serene form. Set in a rose-red Indo-Saracenic complex that is the second-oldest museum in India. A guided hour in this one gallery is worth the whole visit.

venues.n: Fort St George & the Fort Museum
venues.d: Where the East India Company — and modern Chennai — began in 1644, the first English fortress in India and still a working government seat. The Fort Museum keeps colonial portraits, weapons and one of the earliest Union flags; the ramparts and the story of Madras rising from a strip of sand make this the foundation stone of the city.

The oldest Anglican church east of Suez and the oldest surviving British building in India, tucked inside Fort St George — where Robert Clive was married and Elihu Yale, later founder of Yale University, worshipped. The thick bomb-proof walls, old tombstones and quiet interior are a fascinating counterpoint to the Dravidian temples across town.

An 8th-century Pallava temple to Krishna as Parthasarathy — Arjuna's charioteer at Kurukshetra — one of the oldest structures in the city and among the 108 Divya Desams sacred to Vaishnavites. The old Triplicane streets, the vast temple tank and the working ritual life make it a living counterpart to the tourist trail.

A modern multi-tiered temple right on Elliot's Beach dedicated to the eight forms of Lakshmi — goddess of wealth, courage, knowledge and progeny — with shrines rising level upon level and the Bay of Bengal breaking just beyond the walls. Serene, uncrowded and beautiful at sunset; an easy, uplifting stop after a walk on Besant Nagar beach.

An ancient Shiva temple whose name means 'god of medicine' — sages and, by legend, Agastya came here for healing, and devotees still visit for cures. A sprawling Dravidian complex with a great gopuram and tank on the coastal road south, far quieter than Kapaleeshwarar and steeped in the same living ritual.

The great academy of the Indian arts — founded in 1936 by Rukmini Devi Arundale to rescue and revive Bharatanatyam and Carnatic music — set on a serene forty-hectare campus of thatched open-air studios under old trees. Come for a morning dance class in progress, the Rukmini Devi museum, or, if timed right, an evening performance in the theatre. An Institute of National Importance.

A living-history village on the coast road, gathering eighteen authentic historic houses transplanted from across the four southern states — a Chettinad mansion, a Kerala Nair house, weavers' and potters' homes — with craftspeople giving live demonstrations of pottery, weaving and puppetry. The single best half-day for understanding South Indian life; go with the family, closed Tuesdays.

The largest artists' commune in India, founded in 1966 by 38 painters and sculptors from the Madras art school and still owned and run by its members — galleries, studios, a museum and an amphitheatre among casuarina trees near the sea. The birthplace of the Madras Movement in modern Indian art; buy directly from working artists.

260 acres of green quiet on the Adyar estuary — the world headquarters of the Theosophical Society since 1882, with a great library and gardens, and at its heart the Adyar aala maram, a roughly 450-year-old banyan whose aerial roots once shaded 3,000 people. A rare pocket of stillness in the city; note the restricted visiting hours and closure on Sundays.

A monument shaped like a temple chariot honouring Thiruvalluvar, the great Tamil poet-philosopher of the Thirukkural — all 1,330 couplets of his work inscribed on the corridors around a vast auditorium. A striking, purely Tamil piece of civic architecture and a window into the Dravidian pride in language and letters.

The gleaming all-white neoclassical seat of the Chennai Corporation, one of the grandest colonial buildings in the city, crowned by a Westminster-chime clock tower. Best admired from outside as part of a colonial-architecture drive with Central Station and the High Court — the imperial Madras that sits alongside the temples.

The rust-red Indo-Saracenic landmark of the city — a grand 1870s railway terminus with a soaring clock tower, one of the most photographed buildings in South India and the historic gateway to Madras. Even without a train, the façade at dusk is a set-piece of colonial Chennai; pair it with the Ripon Building and the Southern Railway headquarters nearby.

One of the busiest shopping districts in the country and the place Indian families come for weddings — the multi-storey silk emporia of Nalli and Pothys and the vast gold showrooms of GRT and Saravana Stores around Panagal Park. For Kanchipuram silks and temple jewellery there is nowhere denser; a private shopper or advance appointment turns the crush into a calm, seated affair.

The most storied name in South Indian silk — a family house selling Kanchipuram sarees since 1928, its T Nagar flagship the pilgrimage point for brides and connoisseurs seeking hand-woven pure-zari weaves. Ask for the heritage and bridal floors and the master weaves; staff will lay out saree after saree with practised ceremony.

Chennai's original garden-café-and-gallery — a restored colonial mansion set in a lush walled garden, housing the Wild Garden Café, a fashion boutique upstairs, a flower shop and an events folly. The most graceful place in the city for a long lunch or afternoon tea, and a fixture of the design-and-art crowd; leafy, cool and unhurried.

The largest classical arts festival in the world — through December and early January hundreds of Carnatic music and Bharatanatyam concerts fill the sabhas of the city, from the Music Academy to Narada Gana Sabha, alongside the famous canteen food. For anyone who loves Indian classical arts this is the season to come; book the marquee kacheris and a Mylapore canteen table well ahead.

The most prestigious concert hall for Carnatic music in the world — its Sadas and the awarding of the Sangita Kalanidhi title are the highest honour in the tradition, and its December season stage is where reputations are made. Even off-season, catch a recital here to hear the art at its summit; the acoustics and the crowd are the real thing.

venues.n: Filter Coffee & the Mylapore Tiffin Trail
venues.d: The daily ritual of the city: degree filter kaapi frothed between two steel tumblers, and crisp dosai, soft idli and pongal at institutions like Murugan Idli Shop and the old Karpagambal Mess by the temple. Vegetarian, excellent and deeply local — a private food walk through Mylapore's messes and coffee houses is the tastiest hour in Chennai.

The Chennai vegetarian institution that went global — impeccable South Indian tiffin, meals on banana leaf and the full sweep of dosai and filter coffee, born here and now on high streets worldwide. Pure-veg, spotless and reliable across every branch; the original city outlets remain a rite of passage for first-time visitors.

The most celebrated regional cooking of Tamil Nadu — the fiery, aromatic fare of the Chettiar merchant homes, built on freshly roasted spice blends, sun-dried ingredients and dishes like pepper chicken and kara kuzhambu. Seek it at a specialist like The Bangala's Chennai kitchen or a good Chettinad table; a private cook or tasting menu shows its depth beyond the heat.

The oldest hotel in South India — opened in 1854 as the Imperial and reborn as an intimate Art-Deco-and-colonial luxury house after a long restoration — with the storied Verandah for tea and a residents' library that once hosted William Dalrymple. Stay here to sleep inside Madras history; even a drink in the bar is a step into the old city.

Tamil Nadu takes its Ayurveda and siddha traditions seriously, and Chennai's better spas and coastal retreats along the East Coast Road offer authentic panchakarma, abhyanga and consultations with resident vaidyas. A private, physician-led programme — a morning treatment or a multi-day cleanse — is an easy, restorative counterpoint to temples and shopping.

The quieter, cleaner beach the city keeps for itself — 'Bessie' to locals, fronted by the Karl Schmidt memorial and lined with cafés and the Ashtalakshmi temple. Calmer and more polished than the Marina, it's the pleasant end of an evening: a seafront stroll, a coffee, and the sea air.

A rare green lung in the centre of the city — a landscaped botanical garden of some 500 plant species, glasshouses and shaded walks laid out on old colonial nursery grounds. A cool, calm morning stroll between sightseeing, and an easy stop for a multi-generation group needing a gentle interlude.

One of the very few national parks inside a major city — a pocket of dry scrub forest with blackbuck, spotted deer and the adjoining Guindy Snake Park's reptile collection, all within the metropolitan limits. A surprising bit of wild for children and grandparents alike, and a reminder of the country the city grew out of.

A striking circular Marina-front building that once stored ice shipped from America to colonial Madras, later where Swami Vivekananda stayed on his return from Chicago in 1897 — now a museum on his life and Indian philosophy. An unusual, atmospheric stop that ties the seafront to a chapter of India's spiritual renaissance.

The living-history campus doubles as one of the region's best craft-buying stops — resident artisans sell pottery, weaves, puppets and jewellery, and the site runs workshops and rotating exhibitions. A genuine, un-touristy place to pick up handmade South Indian craft with the maker in front of you.

The great Pallava port-city carved from living granite in the 7th and 8th centuries — the Shore Temple standing against the surf, the monolithic Five Rathas, and Arjuna's Penance, one of the largest open-air rock reliefs in the world. A UNESCO World Heritage Site and an unmissable full day; a private guide and an early start beat the coach crowds.

A colossal natural granite boulder poised at an impossible tilt on a smooth slope, unmoved for centuries despite every attempt to shift it — a favourite for photographs and for children who cannot believe it stays put. A short, delightful stop on the Mahabalipuram monument walk.

The oldest temple in Kanchipuram — an 8th-century Pallava sandstone masterpiece to Shiva, its 58 small shrines and delicate carvings a quieter, older beauty than the town's giant later temples. Serene and rarely crowded; the finest single monument for anyone who cares about early Dravidian architecture.

Madras wears its colonial past in stone — the Indo-Saracenic Madras High Court (among the largest court complexes in the world), the University's Senate House, Southern Railway HQ and the Ripon Building. A private morning drive with a heritage guide stitches these red-and-white landmarks into the whole arc from Fort St George to the modern city.

The drive south along the East Coast Road is a pleasure in itself — casuarina groves, the Muttukadu backwater and boating, artisanal spots and quiet resort beaches strung between the city and Mahabalipuram. A relaxed half-day loop with stops at DakshinaChitra and Cholamandal, ending with lunch by the water.
A multi-level design landmark that redefined the city's nightlife — golden bars, open grills and Madras-inspired cocktails under one roof.
A breezy rooftop atop the Hyatt Regency — panoramic city views, resort-style calm and cocktails with a local twist.
A password-only speakeasy behind an unassuming door — a compact, spirited room for craft cocktails and a proper night out.
A music-themed pub of album covers and retro props — craft cocktails, small plates and one of the city's liveliest rooms.
